doc.title: Barry Kernfeld interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 16, 2020

title: Whether jazz is still functional music
summary: Rowe asks if current jazz has functionality; Kernfeld says popular tastes moved to rock, hip hop, disco and DJs, and jazz's era is over.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Okay. Well the more we talk the more I think we have in common, because I had a similar experience in growing up in Rochester with the kind of thing you’re describing so I thank you for sharing that with me. You used the word “functional.” And over my shoulder I have Count Basie and Lester Young and I think of them as playing, I guess, functional music. I mean people could dance to it, they took joy in it, it hit their solar plexuses perhaps more than their head. I’m not sure that’s the way to put it but, so I’m trying to form a question, it has to do with current jazz and I’m wondering if there’s any functionality left in it.

Well I don’t see how there could be because popular tastes have changed several times from the years in which, from the decades in which jazz was the functional music for American society. It was rock. It was hip hop. It was disco. Those are out of order, but it was a whole bunch of things. Rock & roll, since that era, and that’s just practical what people like to do to hang out, what they like to listen to. Now it’s not even live music anymore. What people like to listen to is DJs.
So that’s just — I mean hell, things end. It’s just over.
